facts.statement: Lindwurmia is a rhomaleosaurid plesiosaur that lived in Germany during the Early Jurassic.
facts.quote: Lindwurmia (named after the Lindwurm) is a rhomaleosaurid plesiosaur from the Early Jurassic of Germany.

facts.statement: The genus Lindwurmia contains only one known species, Lindwurmia thiuda.
facts.quote: It contains a single species, Lindwurmia thiuda.

facts.statement: Lindwurmia was a small plesiosaur that measured between 2 and 3 meters in length.
facts.quote: It was a small plesiosaur, measuring 2 to 3 m long.

facts.statement: The holotype of Lindwurmia was discovered in 1899 by Johannes Maak in a clay quarry in Halberstadt, Germany.
facts.quote: It was discovered in the Psiloceras johnstoni ammonite subzone in the clay quarry of Thiemeke'shen Ziegelei in Halberstadt, Germany in 1899 by Johannes Maak

facts.statement: The holotype specimen consists of an incomplete skeleton including sixty-nine vertebrae, jaw fragments, and partial limb girdles.
facts.quote: The holotype is an incomplete postcranium; the anterior section of the jaws, sixty-nine vertebrae, a partial pectoral girdle, pelvic girdles, and the right fore- and hindlimbs.

facts.statement: The specimen was first described by Theodore Brandes in 1912 and 1914.
facts.quote: The specimen was then described by Theodore Brandes, in 1912 and 1914.

facts.statement: Peggy Vincent and Glenn William Storrs formally named the species Lindwurmia thiuda in 2019.
facts.quote: In 2019, Peggy Vincent and Glenn William Storrs named and described the type species Lindwurmia thiuda for the specimen.

facts.statement: Fully grown individuals of Lindwurmia reached a length of approximately 3 meters.
facts.quote: Lindwurmia reached around 3 m long when fully grown.

facts.statement: Research by Vincent and Storrs in 2019 classified Lindwurmia as the sister taxon to Anningasaura within the family Rhomaleosauridae.
facts.quote: Vincent & Storrs (2019) found it to be the sister taxon to Anningasaura within Rhomaleosauridae.

facts.statement: Lindwurmia lived during the Hettangian stage, approximately 201.4 to 199.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Hettangian to Hettangian (201.4 to 199.5 million years ago)

rejected.statement: The skull of Lindwurmia possessed twenty-four cervical vertebrae and five pairs of premaxillary teeth.
rejected.quote: It has twenty-four cervical vertebrae and five pairs of premaxillary teeth.
